newsitem.title: USA: Sales of mini-vans sagging - NYT.
newsitem.headline: Sales of mini-vans sagging - NYT.

text.p: Mini-vans, once the vehicle of choice for suburban moms and dads, appears to be waning in popularity with sales sagging after a decade of steady growth, according to the New York Times.
In the newspaper's Monday editions, the sales decline was attributed to resentment among suburbanites about the image that driving a mini-van projects: a sedate existence.

As they drift away from mini-vans, suburban drivers appear to be snatching up sports utility vehicles. That appears to be the case even though mini-vans tend to be roomier and less expensive than sports utility vehicles.

"The sport utility vehicle is at one end of the spectrum," said Christopher Cedergren, managing director of Nextrends, a Thousand Oaks, California, research group. "It comes across as a rugged, tough vehicle that gives you freedom. The mini-van is at the other end of the spectrum, which would be imprisonment -- with kids and family and responsibility."
Sales of mini-vans dropped four percent last year, and industry analysts said they expect the decline to continue.
"The market is going to be flat or declining," said Susan Jacobs, president of Jacobs & Associates, an automotive strategic planning company in Rutherford, N.J.

Auto makers are responding to the change. General Motors Corp, for example, is putting out Pontiac ads showing cowboys, rather than families with children, gathered around the Montana versio of its Trans Sport mini-van.

The shift in advertising appears to be working. About 60 percent of all Pontiac Trans Sport mini-vans built now are the Montana version and Pontiac plans to increase that to 80 percent, said James Murray, brand manager for the Trans Sport mini-van.
Industry analysts said Chrysler Corp may have the highest risk in this changing market. For years, its vans have accounted for close to half of all mini-vans sold in the United States.

"If the segment isn't expanding and more players come in, the share comes from someone," said James Holden, Chrysler's executive vice president for sales and marketing. "We're going to defend our turf."
